paragraphs.heading: A physical route for carbon
paragraphs.text: The solubility pump is a physical and chemical process that moves carbon from the top of the ocean down into its depths. The carbon travels in a form called dissolved inorganic carbon, or DIC. The pump can work as a sink, taking in some of the carbon dioxide that human activity puts into the air.

paragraphs.heading: Why the deep water is carbon-rich
paragraphs.text: Deep water, the seawater of the ocean's interior, is made at the surface under the same conditions that help carbon dioxide dissolve. So it carries more dissolved inorganic carbon than typical surface water would lead you to expect. Those two processes working together push carbon from the atmosphere down into the interior. The reverse happens too: when deep water rises again in warm waters near the equator, the gas is less soluble there, and the water releases a lot of carbon dioxide back to the air.

paragraphs.heading: Chemistry sets the balance
paragraphs.text: How much carbon dioxide seawater can hold depends on the balance among several carbon-containing forms, and that balance depends on things like pH. Seawater carries positive ions such as sodium and calcium and negative ones such as chloride and sulfate, and normally the positives outweigh the negatives. To make up for that, the carbon forms shift toward negatively charged ones, which lowers the amount of free carbon dioxide in the water. The ocean then takes up more of the gas from the air to restore the balance, so a bigger surplus of positive charge means carbon dioxide dissolves more easily. Chemists call this surplus alkalinity.

paragraphs.heading: Taking up our emissions
paragraphs.text: Burning fossil fuels, changing how land is used and making cement have all sent carbon dioxide into the air. Today roughly a third of these human emissions, about 2 gigatons of carbon a year, is thought to be going into the ocean, and the solubility pump is the main driver of that flow. The human carbon reaches the deep ocean at high latitudes where deep water forms, above all in the North Atlantic.

paragraphs.heading: An uncertain future
paragraphs.text: Most of the carbon dioxide people emit should end up dissolved in the ocean, but how fast that will happen is unclear. One study of the carbon cycle through the 21st century predicted that uptake would level off at a ceiling of 5 gigatons of carbon a year by 2100. A warmer ocean dissolves less carbon dioxide, and warming also layers the ocean more strongly, cutting the surface off from deeper water. A slowdown in the ocean's thermohaline circulation could also mean less dissolved carbon dioxide is carried into the depths, though how large these effects will be is still not known.

paragraphs.heading: A cost and a partner
paragraphs.text: Absorbing more carbon dioxide has a downside: it makes the ocean more acidic, which can cause problems for sea life. The solubility pump also has a living counterpart called the biological pump. Where the solubility pump responds to things like gas exchange and the state of the water, the biological pump is shaped by the marine food web, and it too can change how much carbon dioxide is in the air.
